messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Johnson is a 77-year-old African-American man who has been married for over five decades and currently serves as a school principal. The traumatic event that precipitated his current psychological struggles occurred several months ago when he was assaulted by an armed intruder during one of the school's after-hours events. During the assault, the assailant forced Mr. Johnson to comply with his demands, while drunk and belligerent, creating a situation where Mr. Johnson felt completely powerless and terrified. Since the assault, Mr. Johnson has been struggling with intrusive memories that are triggered by olfactory cues such as the smell of alcohol, which immediately brings back vivid recollections of the event. When he smells alcohol, he is jolted back to the moment when his assailant reeked of liquor. The memory evokes a profound sense of grief and numbness, as if the assault happened to someone else. Each time this happens, it intensifies his feelings of being unable to rely on himself or others for safety. Mr. Johnson's daily routine has been profoundly affected by these triggers. At work, the faint scent of alcohol from a janitorial cleaner can send him into a state of high alert, causing him to scan exits and feel jumpy at any sudden movement nearby. The fear that he might not be able to protect himself or anyone else in such a situation is overwhelming. He has come to believe that the event happened because of his actions—perhaps if he had been more vigilant or assertive, it could have been prevented. This sense of self-blame and reliance on others for safety has become a constant presence in his life. When Mr. Johnson smells alcohol or senses a loss of control, he experiences heightened anxiety, which leads to further negative appraisals about his own capabilities and the unpredictability of others. He feels like he can't trust himself to handle similar situations in the future, and this uncertainty exacerbates his startle response and hypervigilance. Mr. Johnson’s memories are often accompanied by auditory recollections, where sounds from the assault replay in his head. These auditory memories further trigger his grief and numbness, reinforcing his belief that he can't rely on himself or others for protection. The more vivid these memories become, the more he scans exits and feels jumpy, creating a cycle of fear and helplessness. The assault has also strained his relationship with his wife, as he finds it difficult to relax around her when he is triggered by the scent of alcohol or sudden movements. His heightened startle response often leads to him reacting sharply even in safe settings, causing confusion and concern for those around him. What frightens Mr. Johnson most is the possibility that he might never fully recover from this trauma. He fears living with constant hypervigilance and self-doubt, which have already affected his ability to function at work and enjoy life at home. Despite these fears, what brings him to seek help now is a growing realization that he cannot continue living in a state of perpetual anxiety and grief. He hopes for a return to a sense of safety and control over his own life. The trauma has left Mr. Johnson feeling trapped in a cycle where triggers lead to intense threat responses, which in turn feed back into negative self-appraisals and further memory intrusions. This feedback loop is the central challenge he faces as he begins to explore treatment options. He hopes that through therapy, he can regain some control over his memories and fears, ultimately finding relief from the constant reminders of the assault and a return to a sense of safety in his daily life.
